title: Present Perfect or Past Simple: Time Matters
summary: Choose the past simple for finished times and the present perfect for experiences or situations that reach the present. Ask about the exact past time with the past simple.
learningObjectives: Use the past simple with finished-time expressions such as yesterday and last weekend.
Use the present perfect for past experiences without a specified finished time and for current results.
Form When and What time questions about finished events in the past simple.
Distinguish a continuing period from a period that ended in the past.

explanation.heading: Finished time: past simple
explanation.body: Use the past simple with an event at a finished time, such as yesterday, on Tuesday, last year or two days ago. Do not use the present perfect with these explicit finished-time expressions.
explanation.example: We watched a documentary on Saturday night.

explanation.heading: Time up to now: present perfect
explanation.body: Use have or has plus the past participle to describe experiences up to now, or past actions whose result matters now, without placing the action at a finished time. Ever and yet often appear in this use.
explanation.example: Have you ever ridden a horse?

explanation.heading: Ask when with the past simple
explanation.body: Use When did ...? or What time did ...? to ask for a particular completed past time. After did, use the base form of the main verb, not its past participle.
explanation.example: What time did the match finish?

explanation.heading: Current result versus past detail
explanation.body: A present perfect sentence can introduce a recent development or a present result. When you add a finished past time, switch to the past simple. A conversation may naturally use both forms.
explanation.example: I have found my headphones. They were under the sofa yesterday.

explanation.heading: Still true or already finished
explanation.body: Present perfect with for or since can describe how long a situation has continued until now. The past simple describes how long a situation lasted when it is over. Make the timeline clear in your choice.
explanation.example: Nora has worked here for a year, but her brother worked here for a year and then moved away.

comparisons.title: Experience up to now versus a finished visit

left.label: present perfect
left.note: The question covers experiences at any time up to now.

right.label: past simple
right.example: Did you try kayaking on your holiday last month?
right.note: The question is about a particular completed time.

left.label: still true now
left.example: Farah has lived in Leeds for four years.

right.label: finished in the past
right.example: Farah lived in York for four years.
right.note: She no longer lives in York.

examples.sentence: I bought my new coat last Friday.
examples.note: Last Friday is a finished time, so use the past simple.

examples.sentence: My uncle has travelled to several countries.
examples.note: The sentence describes his experience up to now without specifying when.

examples.sentence: When did you first meet your neighbour?
examples.note: A When question about a particular past event uses did plus the base verb.

examples.sentence: The parcel has arrived, so we can open it now.
examples.note: The completed arrival matters because of its result now.

examples.sentence: My parents lived near the coast for ten years, but they moved inland in 2021.
examples.note: A completed period uses the past simple, even though it lasted many years.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I have visited my cousins yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: Yesterday is a finished time, so the verb must be past simple.

commonMistakes.incorrect: When have you sent the message?
commonMistakes.correct: When did you send the message?
commonMistakes.why: To ask about the specific past time, use did plus the base form send.
A situation beginning in the past and still true now uses the present perfect.
The present perfect uses have plus the past participle gone, not the past form went.

studyTips: Look for an explicit finished-time expression: yesterday, last month and ago usually require the past simple.
Use the question “When exactly?” to recognise when the past simple is needed.
Ask whether a situation still continues: if it does, the present perfect with for or since is often appropriate.

exercises.prompt: I ___ my jacket on the bus yesterday.
choices: left
have left
leave
exercises.feedback: Yesterday is a finished time, so use the past simple left.

exercises.prompt: I ___ in this neighbourhood since 2022, and I still live here.
choices: lived
have lived
was living
exercises.feedback: Since 2022 together with still live describes a situation continuing up to now.

exercises.prompt: What time ___ the last bus last night?
choices: has it left
it has left
did it leave
exercises.feedback: Last night is a finished time. Ask What time did it leave? using the base verb.

choices: Did your train arrive
Has your train arrived
Does your train arrived
exercises.feedback: Yesterday requires a past-simple question with did and the base form arrive.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the past simple of buy: “We ___ this sofa last Saturday.”
exercises.feedback: Last Saturday specifies a finished past time, so use bought.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the present perfect of visit, including the auxiliary: “I ___ that museum several times in my life.”
exercises.feedback: The sentence summarises experiences up to now without a specific finished time.

exercises.prompt: Complete the past-simple question with did and the correct verb: “When ___ your new colleague?”
exercises.feedback: When asks about a finished past event; did takes the base form meet.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the negative present perfect of finish: “Lara ___ her dinner yet.”
exercises.feedback: Yet focuses on what has not happened up to now, so use has not finished.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We have watched a film last Friday.
acceptedAnswers: We watched a film last Friday.
exercises.feedback: Last Friday is a finished time; change have watched to watched.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Did you ever been to Wales?
acceptedAnswers: Have you ever been to Wales?
exercises.feedback: An experience up to now uses have you ever been, not did you ever been.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Have you bought your laptop yesterday?
acceptedAnswers: Did you buy your laptop yesterday?
exercises.feedback: A question about yesterday uses Did you buy, not Have you bought.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Max has lived in Rome for two years, but he moved to Dublin last month.
acceptedAnswers: Max lived in Rome for two years, but he moved to Dublin last month.
exercises.feedback: His time in Rome has ended; use the past simple lived for that completed period.

speakingExercises.prompt: Leo lost his phone yesterday. Report this finished past event in one sentence.
speakingExercises.feedback: Yesterday marks a finished time, so use the past simple lost.

speakingExercises.prompt: Mina started working here in 2023 and still works here. Say one sentence using the present perfect and since.
speakingExercises.feedback: Has worked describes a situation continuing to now; since marks the starting year.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask a friend about the experience of trying skiing at any time in their life. Use ever and the present perfect.
speakingExercises.feedback: Have you ever tried asks about experience up to the present, with no finished time.

speakingExercises.prompt: The train is at the station now. Report this new result in one sentence beginning “The train”, using the present perfect of arrive.
speakingExercises.feedback: Has arrived reports a completed action with a present result: the train is here now.

speakingExercises.prompt: Change “Dina has painted the door” into a sentence saying the action happened last Friday. Use the past simple and keep the same subject and object.
acceptedAnswers: Dina painted the door last Friday.
speakingExercises.feedback: Last Friday is a finished time, so use the past simple painted.

speakingExercises.prompt: A friend asks, “When did Nora leave?” Nora left at seven last night. Answer in one sentence beginning “Nora left” and give the time.
acceptedAnswers: Nora left at seven last night.
speakingExercises.feedback: Use left, the past simple of leave, for a specific completed time last night.

speakingExercises.prompt: You want to know the exact date when a new bridge opened. Correct this question: “When have they opened the new bridge?” Say the entire question with did.
acceptedAnswers: When did they open the new bridge?
speakingExercises.feedback: For a specific past time, ask When did ...? and use the base form open after did.

speakingExercises.prompt: A package is at your house now; it came yesterday morning. Say exactly two sentences beginning “The package” and “It”. First report its arrival using the present perfect. Then say when it came using the past simple.
acceptedAnswers: The package has arrived. It came yesterday morning.
The package's arrived. It came yesterday morning.
speakingExercises.feedback: Has arrived announces a result now; came yesterday morning gives the finished past-time detail.

listeningExercises.audioText: I haven't read that book yet.
choices: The speaker finished the book last week.
The speaker has not read it up to now.
The speaker read it yesterday.
listeningExercises.feedback: Haven't read ... yet describes something that has not happened up to now.

listeningExercises.audioText: We visited the aquarium on Tuesday afternoon.
listeningExercises.prompt: When did the visit take place?
choices: At an unspecified time in the speaker’s life.
At some point in the future.
On a particular afternoon in the past.
listeningExercises.feedback: On Tuesday afternoon identifies a completed past time, so the speaker uses visited.

listeningExercises.audioText: I haven't sent the invitations yet.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type only the final word you hear.
listeningExercises.feedback: Yet in a negative present perfect sentence means the action has not happened up to now.

listeningExercises.audioText: The neighbours have finally fixed the lift, so everyone can use it again.
listeningExercises.prompt: What has changed for people in the building?
choices: They must wait for the repair to begin.
They can travel between floors in a working lift.
The lift has broken down for the first time.
listeningExercises.feedback: Have fixed signals a completed repair with a result now: the lift can be used again.

listeningExercises.audioText: I have seen that play twice, but I first saw it in May.
listeningExercises.prompt: What happened during the month mentioned?
choices: The speaker saw the play for the first time.
The speaker decided never to watch the play.
The speaker bought tickets for a future show.
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker has seen the play twice in total; the first visit took place in May.

listeningExercises.audioText: Kim worked at the station for two years before leaving last month. She has lived in this town for ten years.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which situation is still true now?
choices: Kim still works at the station.
Kim left the town last month.
Kim continues to live in the town.
listeningExercises.feedback: Worked ... before leaving describes an ended job, but has lived ... for ten years describes a continuing home.

listeningExercises.audioText: She's found the missing receipt, so we can leave now.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type only the contracted first word you hear, including its apostrophe.
listeningExercises.feedback: She’s means she has here, followed by the past participle found; it is present perfect.

listeningExercises.audioText: We picked up the chairs after lunch yesterday.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type only the two-word past-simple verb phrase immediately after the subject.
listeningExercises.feedback: Picked up is the past-simple verb phrase, appropriate with yesterday.
